pyharp computes radiative fluxes with one of two solvers: the two-stream solver of Toon et al. (`solver: toon`)
and the multi-stream discrete-ordinate solver DISORT (`solver: disort`). This chapter measures how accurate each is
and what it costs. It first fixes a reference: DISORT run with enough streams that adding more no longer changes
the fluxes, validated against published benchmark fluxes and against cases with a closed-form answer. It then
measures Toon against that reference and separates two errors that are easy to confuse: the error of solving the
two-stream equations, which is round-off, and the error of the two-stream approximation itself, which is not. It
ends with the cost per column of each solver. The derivations of the two solvers are not repeated here; they are
the subject of the DISORT and Toon chapters.

@fig-ch05-map shows how the sections depend on each other, and @tbl-ch05-schemes lists them.

Every number, table and figure of this chapter is regenerated by one command, `derivation-checks/ch05_run.sh
<venv>`, which runs the five checks and rewrites their outputs and the figure data. The environment it needs is
built from public pins only by `derivation-checks/ch05_setup.sh`: pyharp at the code pin, pydisort 1.7.1 from its
published wheel checked by hash, and torch 2.10.0 with CUDA 12.6. With an nvcc older than 12.8 that script applies
one patch to pyharp's CMake list of CUDA architectures, `derivation-checks/ch05_setup/cuda-arch-sm120.patch`,
without which the CUDA build fails; it touches no source file. The second line of every output records the
pyharp and pydisort commits, the torch build, the CPU, the GPU and the compilers of the run.
